evidence.excerpt: This book will help you find the weak part instead of blaming “AI” as though it were one indivisible object. Read the chapters in order to build the complete picture. Use the separate Concept Index when you need to look up one term—such as token, context, memory, routing or agent—and then jump to the chapter where that term does real work.

This is the first lesson of the whole book: the quality of an AI result depends on more than the wording of one prompt. It depends on what the system is trying to help you do, what information reached it, what operations ran, what the model produced and what you checked before acting.

Later chapters will open each part carefully: how models are trained and run; how tokens and context windows affect what fits; how session and memory differ; what retrieval, tools, permissions, routing and wrappers add; how agents and multi-step loops work; and why convincing answers can still fail. The Concept Index will let you find any one term without turning the book itself into a dictionary.

You did not consult one all-knowing thing. You used an **AI system**: the whole working arrangement that received your request and produced the result. That arrangement includes the product you opened, the instructions and material available for this task, at least one trained model, and the software that presents the answer. Some systems can also search, calculate, retrieve documents or take actions. The exact arrangement varies from product to product.

The **model** is an important part of that system, but it is not the whole system. It is the trained component that processes input and produces an output. The product and surrounding software shape what reaches it, which other capabilities are available and what you eventually see.
We will begin with one decision and follow it all the way through. Nothing floats around as a loose definition. Every part earns its name by changing what happens next.

Not every AI product has the same tools, and not every available tool runs on every request. The useful question is not “Does this AI have tools?” It is “What operation actually ran for this answer, and can I inspect what came back?”

1. **What decision am I actually trying to make?** If the system solved a narrower problem, restate the real one.
2. **What information did this answer actually use?** Check the messages, files, dates and missing facts that mattered.
3. **What current source or operation supports the consequential claims?** Inspect the returned evidence; do not treat fluency as a citation.
4. **What must remain my decision or another person’s responsibility?** Name the value judgment, permission or professional check that cannot be delegated.

aiEditorialAnalysis.prompt: Why doesn't the record of 5,944 non-affirmations mean 5,944 Medicare patients were denied care?
aiEditorialAnalysis.response: A non-affirmation is an early-stage payment decision, not a final outcome: it means the submitted paperwork did not satisfy Medicare's rules at that checkpoint. CMS says a licensed clinician, not the AI alone, determines any non-payment recommendation, and the request can still be corrected, resubmitted or appealed — the payment records themselves only count savings when none of those reversals happen. Providers can also skip prior authorization and be reviewed after the service is delivered but before payment.

aiEditorialAnalysis.assessment: The article's mechanism fully supports this answer in ordinary language; every element of the explain-back is traceable to P003, P005 and P006, so the outcome passes.

aiEditorialAnalysis.prompt: Using this article's mechanism, what should a reader check before accepting that 48,000 claims were rejected?
aiEditorialAnalysis.response: First check whether the cited table counts total processed decisions or only adverse ones — the WISeR table labeled 20,397 'decisions' included 14,453 approvals. Second, check whether a 'rejection' at that stage is final or an intermediate status that can be corrected, resubmitted or appealed, and whether a human reviewer signs off on adverse outcomes. Third, look for separate evidence of real operational harm — aging queues, systems launched before they were functional — which can be true even when the headline number is wrong.

Page 322, Table 2 lists 20,397 year-to-date decisions received for Virtix and Zyter through the March 30, 2026 report: 6,096 for Virtix and 14,301 for Zyter. Page 322, Table 3 splits those 20,397 decisions into 14,453 affirmations and 5,944 non-affirmations. Virtix has 2,863 affirmations and 3,233 non-affirmations; Zyter has 11,590 affirmations and 2,711 non-affirmations. Page 22 says payment savings are calculated from non-affirmations not followed by an affirmed resubmission or a successfully appealed claim denial. It also says one series of non-affirmations for the same beneficiary, item or service, and provider within 120 days earns only one participant payment. Page 234 says that as of March 30 Genzeon had 123 prior-authorization requests aged three days or older, with the oldest 83 days. It separates them into 14 awaiting a model-participant response, 44 awaiting a decision letter and 65 awaiting correction for creation of a tracking number or dismissal. The page does not say which stage applied to the oldest request. In a December 12, 2025 letter on pages 216 and 217, Innovaccer said it would meet the January 5, 2026 go-live date without full functionality. It cited changing requirements, new integration expectations, unclear governance and insufficient end-to-end testing time, and planned to auto-affirm requests while completing a phased rollout. Page 217 says Innovaccer expected the initial auto-affirmation period to last approximately 45 to 60 days and described the approach as a way to avoid a backlog of unprocessed requests while it finished, validated and deployed the full rules-based solution. Page 99 sets quality multipliers at 100 percent for aggregate scores of 85 to 100 percent, 95 percent for scores of 60 to 84 percent and 90 percent below 60 percent. It also says CMS conducts quarterly audits of participant records for consistency with Original Medicare coverage criteria. Page 410 groups January requests for two vendors into one-to-five, six-to-ten and eleven-to-twenty-one-day buckets. Those buckets do not disclose an exact rate for responses inside or outside 72 hours.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: Prior authorization means a provider asks before treatment for assurance that Medicare will pay. In WISeR, a participating company uses AI and other technology to review whether documentation meets Medicare rules; CMS says a licensed clinician determines any recommendation not to pay.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: The WISeR Model helps protect American taxpayers by leveraging enhanced technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), along with human clinical review, to ensure timely and appropriate Medicare payment for select items and services. WISeR will run for six performance years from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2031 in six states: New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona, and Washington. WISeR does not change Medicare coverage or payment policy. The model excludes inpatient-only services, emergency services, and services that would pose a substantial risk to patients if delayed. All recommendations for non-payment are determined by appropriately licensed clinicians who will apply standardized, transparent and evidence-based procedures to their review. WISeR does not apply to people with Medicare Advantage and will have no impact on them. Providers and suppliers for people with Original Medicare in selected regions will have the choice of submitting a prior authorization request for the model’s selected items and services or going through a post-service/pre-payment review. Model participants receive a percentage of the expenditures associated with averted wasteful, inappropriate care as a result of their reviews. That percentage is adjusted based on the participant’s performance on measures related to the process, including provider experience.

Current primary program description for WISeR scope, review mechanism, safeguards, participants and payment design. Limitation: This is CMS's current description of its own model and safeguards. It does not answer each problem in the released records or independently establish how well every vendor followed the requirements.

claimMap.scopeAndFreshness: CMS's model page says all non-payment recommendations are determined by appropriately licensed clinicians; P005 correctly attributes this to CMS rather than asserting it independently.

candidateEvidence.excerpt: The useful distinction is between a payment checkpoint and a treatment decision: a payment review can delay care, but it is not the same as an AI choosing a treatment. Providers can instead proceed to review after service and before payment.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: KFF reported on June 23 that patients, doctors and other health professionals it interviewed described confusion, errors, long waits and stress during WISeR's rollout. KFF reported that an Oklahoma Medicare beneficiary made an extra two-and-a-half-hour drive after learning his regular procedure needed preapproval and declined a proposed third trip that he understood was for paperwork. Humata CEO Jeremy Friese told KFF that its system gives an ‘immediate yes’ in 88 percent of cases for which clinical data supports an approval. Zyter CEO Sundar Subramanian told KFF that the company continuously monitors operations and works with stakeholders to address questions and improve provider experience. CMS official Abe Sutton told KFF that the model aims to reduce inappropriate care without delaying appropriate care and that payment backlogs were being resolved. KFF reported clinicians' suspicion of AI-generated errors, while Humata's CEO said he had not heard about AI hallucinations.

Independent June 23 reporting for patient/provider experience, CMS and vendor responses, and program background before the September records release. Limitation: This is June background, not new September reporting. The reported experiences establish real concerns and attributed accounts, not that AI caused every delay, that every non-affirmation was wrong or that the same conditions continued unchanged through September.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: KFF reported on June 23 that patients, doctors and other health professionals it interviewed described confusion, errors, long waits and stress during WISeR's rollout. KFF reported that an Oklahoma Medicare beneficiary made an extra two-and-a-half-hour drive after learning his regular procedure needed preapproval and declined a proposed third trip that he understood was for paperwork. Humata CEO Jeremy Friese told KFF that its system gives an ‘immediate yes’ in 88 percent of cases for which clinical data supports an approval. Zyter CEO Sundar Subramanian told KFF that the company continuously monitors operations and works with stakeholders to address questions and improve provider experience. CMS official Abe Sutton told KFF that the model aims to reduce inappropriate care without delaying appropriate care and that payment backlogs were being resolved. KFF reported clinicians' suspicion of AI-generated errors, while Humata's CEO said he had not heard about AI hallucinations.

Independent June 23 reporting for patient/provider experience, CMS and vendor responses, and program background before the September records release. Limitation: This is June background, not new September reporting. The reported experiences establish real concerns and attributed accounts, not that AI caused every delay, that every non-affirmation was wrong or that the same conditions continued unchanged through September.

claimMap.scopeAndFreshness: Humata CEO's 88 percent 'immediate yes' claim and Zyter's stakeholder-engagement statement both appear in KFF's reporting exactly as attributed in P009.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: Page 322, Table 2 lists 20,397 year-to-date decisions received for Virtix and Zyter through the March 30, 2026 report: 6,096 for Virtix and 14,301 for Zyter. Page 322, Table 3 splits those 20,397 decisions into 14,453 affirmations and 5,944 non-affirmations. Virtix has 2,863 affirmations and 3,233 non-affirmations; Zyter has 11,590 affirmations and 2,711 non-affirmations. Page 22 says payment savings are calculated from non-affirmations not followed by an affirmed resubmission or a successfully appealed claim denial. It also says one series of non-affirmations for the same beneficiary, item or service, and provider within 120 days earns only one participant payment. Page 234 says that as of March 30 Genzeon had 123 prior-authorization requests aged three days or older, with the oldest 83 days. It separates them into 14 awaiting a model-participant response, 44 awaiting a decision letter and 65 awaiting correction for creation of a tracking number or dismissal. The page does not say which stage applied to the oldest request. In a December 12, 2025 letter on pages 216 and 217, Innovaccer said it would meet the January 5, 2026 go-live date without full functionality. It cited changing requirements, new integration expectations, unclear governance and insufficient end-to-end testing time, and planned to auto-affirm requests while completing a phased rollout. Page 217 says Innovaccer expected the initial auto-affirmation period to last approximately 45 to 60 days and described the approach as a way to avoid a backlog of unprocessed requests while it finished, validated and deployed the full rules-based solution. Page 99 sets quality multipliers at 100 percent for aggregate scores of 85 to 100 percent, 95 percent for scores of 60 to 84 percent and 90 percent below 60 percent. It also says CMS conducts quarterly audits of participant records for consistency with Original Medicare coverage criteria. Page 410 groups January requests for two vendors into one-to-five, six-to-ten and eleven-to-twenty-one-day buckets. Those buckets do not disclose an exact rate for responses inside or outside 72 hours.

Primary documents for the payment design, audit safeguard, pre-launch vendor warning and dated operational tables cited in the article. Limitation: The review was bounded to seven cited pages plus direct checks of the complete file's identity and page count, not a claim to have substantively reviewed every one of 443 pages. Operational tables are dated snapshots and some are cumulative; they must not be added together. Non-affirmation is not synonymous with a final denial of care.
